bills.headline: Vetoed bill would have expanded Georgia's historic rehabilitation tax credit for commercial structures.
bills.recap: This bill would have raised the yearly cap on historic rehab tax credits for non-home historic buildings from $30 million to $60 million. It would also have raised the per-project cap for large job-creating projects from $10 million to $15 million. For non-home structures, the credit rate would have dropped from 25% to 20%, plus an extra 10% in counties under 50,000 people. The minimum spending to qualify would have risen from $5,000 to $25,000. Historic home credits stayed largely the same. The governor vetoed the bill, so current rules remain in place, which matters for agents working with investors or buyers of historic properties.

bills.headline: Requires HOAs to register with the state and adds new homeowner protections.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, homeowner and condo associations must register each year with the Secretary of State ($100 fee) before they can collect fines or fees, file liens, or foreclose. Associations that opt out cannot charge fines, fees, or accelerated assessments. Owners gain a list of rights, including access to three years of financial records, a state complaint process that pauses collection of disputed fines, and a rule that payments go to regular dues first, then special assessments, then fines. HOA lien foreclosures now require 60 days' notice and a higher minimum debt that excludes fines, and starting July 1, 2026, associations must give written notice and 30 days to pay before collecting attorney's fees; judges can also seal certain eviction records, which matters for buyers, sellers, and renters in HOA communities.

bills.title: "Georgia Property Owners' Bill of Rights Act"; enact

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The committee version lets an HOA choose not to register with the Secretary of State, but an unregistered HOA could not collect fines or fees. Registered HOAs would only need to register before collecting fines or fees, filing liens, or foreclosing, not before collecting dues. The complaint board gets more power: it can hold hearings, impose civil fines, issue cease-and-desist orders, and hear owner complaints filed within 180 days, with appeals to superior court. The new version also makes HOAs apply owner payments to dues first, then fees, then fines. It drops the earlier ban on the HOA and its insiders bidding at foreclosure sales. It sets the foreclosure minimum at the lesser of $4,000 or 12 months of past-due dues, not counting collection fees or fines, and extends the lien life from four to six years. The owner rights list no longer includes one vote per lot or the rights to display flags, political signs, and religious or holiday signs.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The Senate passed this version with two real changes; the rest is formatting and line numbering. First, members of the new state complaint board for property owners' associations cannot work for, or have major business ties with, a law firm that represents association boards or a property management firm that serves associations. Second, the foreclosure threshold is clarified: an association can foreclose on a lot owner's lien only if the amount owed is the lesser of $4,000 or 12 months of past-due dues, and that amount must also be at least $2,000, not counting collection fees or fines.
versions.name: Engrossed

versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee version drops the proposed five-member state complaint review board. Instead, homeowners file complaints with the Secretary of State, who appoints a hearing officer. Appeals go to magistrate court for smaller amounts or superior court for larger ones, and the losing side pays a $100 fee. It also covers common interest communities, requires associations to file their governing documents when they register, defines regular, special, and specific assessments, and bans accelerated assessments and refusing partial payments. Payments must now go first to regular dues, then special assessments, then specific assessments, then fees and fines, unless an association's declaration recorded by June 30, 2026 says otherwise. For foreclosure, notice time grows from 30 to 90 days, and paying within 90 days stops the foreclosure. Owners can get a one-time stay of up to 90 days while an appeal is pending, and the association can bid only up to the lien amount. Before an association can collect attorney's fees, it must send a certified notice, give the owner 30 days to pay, and provide an itemized fee list, and a judge must find the fees reasonable. Most of the bill takes effect January 1, 2027, and the attorney's fee rules take effect July 1, 2026. The satellite dish right was removed.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: This newer version (a Rules Committee substitute) keeps the core HOA plan: associations must register with the Secretary of State, owners can file complaints and get hearings, owners get a set of listed rights, and payments must go to regular dues first. Filing a complaint now automatically pauses collection of the disputed fines or fees until the hearing officer rules, and owners can also see the HOA's bank statements. The foreclosure notice period rises from 30 to 60 days instead of the 90 days in the prior version, and the one-time pause of foreclosure during an appeal is dropped. New sections let existing HOAs opt into the Georgia Property Owners' Association Act with an 80 percent vote, add an emergency exception to the attorney's fee notice rules, remove protection for older declarations on payment order, and let courts seal certain eviction records when the tenant wins, pays in full, or after seven years.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced version and the enrolled version. The differences are only formatting: an updated document code, a new header listing the sponsors and marking the bill "As Passed," and page labels. The substance of the bill, including the HOA registration rules, owner rights, lien limits, and eviction record changes, stays the same.

bills.headline: Property owners can claim compensation from local governments for lost value due to nonenforcement.
bills.recap: Owners or leaseholders can file a written claim with their city or county if it has a pattern of not enforcing laws on things like illegal camping, loitering, panhandling, drug use or shoplifting. Claims can also be filed for violating state immigration sanctuary rules or for maintaining a public nuisance. Owners can seek either documented costs to deal with the problem or the drop in fair market value. Payment is capped at the local property taxes paid on the parcel the prior year, and owners can sue in superior court if the claim is denied or ignored for 30 days. Realtors may see owners citing nearby conditions and value impacts, and appraisals may play a role in these claims.

bills.title: Local government; procedures for real property owners to make claims for compensation for loss of property value or expenses incurred; provisions

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The committee version narrows when property owners can claim money from a city or county for lost property value or costs caused by non-enforcement of laws (like illegal camping or panhandling) or a public nuisance. It defines "policy, pattern, or practice" as a widespread, organized practice, so one-off or isolated failures do not count. It caps payments at the property taxes that local government collected over the prior two years, leaving out school taxes, and lets the government defend itself by showing it took reasonable steps to address the nuisance. It also makes an owner pay the government's legal fees if they keep filing after two unsuccessful claims on the same property, and it says claims are handled under an existing tax refund process (Code Section 48-5-380).
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new substitute changes the claim deadline. Owners now must file within the same tax year the events happened, instead of within 24 months. It also changes the payment cap: compensation can't exceed the local property taxes paid on the parcel in the prior tax year, instead of the old cap tied to taxes from the two years before the claim. Owners whose claims are denied as incomplete may now revise and resubmit them. The penalty for repeat claims is tougher: after just one unsuccessful claim on a parcel (down from two), the local government recovers its legal fees and costs on any later failed claim. Repeat claims in later years now require ongoing money damages rather than just 'injury,' and the rest of the changes are wording cleanups and a new Code section number.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edit is to the header: the line naming the House Committee on Public Safety and Homeland Security as the source of the substitute was replaced with the bill number and a list of sponsors, including Representatives Gaines, Leverett, Crowe, Jones, and Anderson. The rules on how property owners can claim compensation for lost property value or expenses were not changed.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The final version keeps the core plan: property owners can ask their city or county to pay them back for cleanup costs or lost property value caused by things like ignored illegal camping, panhandling, or immigration sanctuary policies, capped at the prior year's local property taxes. New sections let anyone harmed by a local sanctuary policy, or by a jail that ignores a federal immigration detainer, ask a superior court to order compliance, and those cases get priority. The rule making repeat losing claimants pay the local government's legal fees now applies only to claims that were complete when filed, so incomplete paperwork won't count against an owner. The bill title also mentions public disclosure of certain state documents, but no section in this version actually does that.

bills.headline: Lets owners of business personal property over $200,000 appeal tax values to a hearing officer.
bills.recap: This law adds a new appeal option for taxpayers with business personal property, such as equipment, valued over $200,000 on their assessment notice. They can now take value or uniformity disputes to a hearing officer instead of the county board of equalization. Former or current Appraiser IV or chief appraisers can apply to the Georgia Real Estate Commission and Appraisers Board to serve as these hearing officers, but not in counties where they worked. It also narrows the 'public utility' definition so private water and sewer systems count only if they have at least 10,000 connections. That change could affect how smaller private systems serving neighborhoods are taxed.

bills.headline: Cuts Georgia income tax rates, raises deductions, and repeals many tax credits and exemptions.
bills.recap: Despite its title about a senior homestead exemption, the final law is a broad income tax package. It cuts the personal income tax rate to 4.99% for 2026, with yearly cuts toward 3.99% if state revenue allows. It also raises the standard and dependent deductions, raises the retirement income exclusion for those 65 and older, and exempts some overtime and cash tips. It repeals a number of business tax credits and sales tax exemptions, including one for machinery, equipment, and materials used to build or operate certain buildings, which could affect some construction costs, while lower income taxes may give buyers a bit more room in their budgets.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; certain senior citizens who volunteer with local governments; provide homestead exemption

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The House Ways and Means Committee version drops a condition that tied this bill to a separate constitutional amendment. That amendment would have let local governments offer a homestead exemption for value increases above inflation, and it had to pass in November 2026. Now the senior volunteer homestead exemption only needs approval from voters in the statewide referendum. If voters approve, it takes effect January 1, 2027, and the exemption itself is unchanged: up to $500 or the tax owed per year, whichever is less.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edit is to the header: it now lists the bill's sponsors (Representatives Blackmon, Burns, Hatchett, Gilliard, Stephens, and others) instead of saying the House Ways and Means Committee offered the substitute. The rules for the senior volunteer homestead exemption are the same.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee replaced the whole bill with a different subject. The old version created an optional local homestead exemption of up to $500 for seniors 65 and older who volunteer with local governments, and it needed a statewide vote in November 2026. That is gone. The new version cuts Georgia income taxes instead: the personal rate drops to 4.99% for 2026, 4.49% for 2027, and 3.99% from 2028 on, though later cuts can be delayed if state revenue or reserves fall short. Corporate, S-corporation, and electing partnership rates follow the personal rate. The standard deduction rises from $24,000 to $32,000 for joint filers and from $12,000 to $16,000 for single filers. The changes take effect July 1, 2026 and apply to tax years starting January 1, 2026.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The final version is much broader than the Senate committee version. Both versions cut the state income tax rate, but the final bill sets the 2026 rate at 4.99% and lowers it by 0.125% a year down to 3.99%, instead of using fixed yearly steps. The standard deduction is now $30,000 for joint filers and $15,000 for single filers, rising each year to $36,000 and $18,000, and the dependent deduction rises from $4,000 to $5,000 and then up to $6,000; these increases can be delayed if state revenue falls short. New items include a higher retirement income exclusion for people 65 or older ($70,000 starting in 2027), tax breaks of up to $1,750 each on overtime pay and cash tips through 2028, a larger state rainy-day fund cap with extra money usable for tax relief, and repeal of several business tax credits and sales tax exemptions, including credits for electric vehicles and teleworking.

bills.headline: Raises Georgia's bankruptcy homestead exemption from $21,500 to $50,000, with inflation increases.
bills.recap: This law raises the amount of equity a person can protect in their home, co-op, or burial plot in bankruptcy from $21,500 to $50,000. If the home is titled to one spouse who is the debtor and it is both spouses' primary residence, the protected amount rises from $43,000 to $100,000. Starting July 1, 2031, both amounts will be adjusted each year for inflation, using a method set by the state revenue commissioner. Realtors may see financially struggling homeowners keep more of their equity, which could affect distressed sales and how creditors pursue homes.

bills.headline: Requires human trafficking training for hotel staff and third-party short-term rental managers.
bills.recap: Starting July 1, 2026, on-site hotel employees and paid third-party managers of short-term rentals must take yearly human trafficking awareness training approved by the Attorney General's office. Owners, operators, or managers must adopt reporting policies, post required trafficking notices, and keep training records for the length of employment plus one year. Willful violations can bring fines of $500, $1,000, and then $2,000 for repeat offenses. Owners who manage their own rentals, and rentals offered fewer than 15 days a year, are exempt, so Realtors and brokers who manage short-term rentals for clients should take note.

bills.recap: This law adds code enforcement officials to the list of workers with extra protection under Georgia's assault and battery laws. bills.headline: Updates Georgia transfer-on-death deed rules for passing real estate at death.
bills.recap: Despite its title, this law mainly changes Georgia's transfer-on-death deeds, which let owners name who gets their property at death. Each beneficiary must sign and record an affidavit, now including the deed book and page, within nine months of death or the property goes back to the estate. The estate can pay mortgage, taxes, and urgent repairs before acceptance and gets a lien to be repaid, and an insolvent estate may sell the property facing foreclosure or condemnation. Revocation now needs only one witness plus an officer, sale of the property revokes the TOD deed, and the law also limits local rules on livestock; agents handling inherited property should watch these title and timing rules.

bills.headline: Creates a local sales tax to cut homestead property taxes and limits local tax hikes.
bills.lastAction: House Agreed Senate Amend or Sub As Amended
bills.recap: The bill lets each county hold a referendum to adopt a 1 percent Local Homestead Option Sales Tax starting in 2028. The money would fund an extra homestead exemption on primary homes and up to five acres, and it would replace any existing HOST in that county. Starting in 2027, school boards and local governments could not raise property tax revenue by more than 3 percent or inflation, whichever is greater, without voter or legislative approval. It also bars back-billing owners for a homestead exemption applied by mistake through no fault of their own, and requires income-producing property owners to share income and expense data with assessors on request. Realtors may care because lower and more predictable homestead tax bills can affect affordability and the cost of owning a home.

bills.title: Homeownership Opportunity and Market Equalization Act of 2026; enact

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The committee version greatly expands the bill: the statewide homestead exemption still rises in steps ($10,000 in 2027–28, $30,000 in 2029–30, $60,000 in 2031), but now fully exempts the home's value starting in 2032, with some local opt-out delays. Starting in 2032, new homestead owners would pay full property tax in their first year before the exemption begins, and major improvements would be fully taxed in the year they are first assessed. The new version adds a Local Homestead Option Sales Tax (LHOST) to pay for these exemptions, raises the overall local sales tax cap from 2% to 5% starting July 2027, allows SPLOST and LOST at rates below 1%, and creates non-property-based 'local finance assessments' that must be paid or the owner loses homestead exemptions. It also softens the failure-to-report penalty to a flat 50%, ties the voter-approval budget cap to the greater of 3% or inflation (with a local Act as another option), drops the earlier tax bill, notice, and newspaper-error changes, and makes major parts depend on voters passing a constitutional amendment.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new version drops the plan to phase in a full statewide homestead exemption, the first-year tax on new owners after a sale, the local 'finance assessments,' and the voter approval rule for big school and local budget increases. Instead, homestead property would be assessed at a lower share of market value, falling 3 percent a year starting in 2027 until it reaches 10 percent of fair market value (down from today's 40 percent), if voters approve a constitutional amendment. LOST and HOST sales taxes would convert into a new local homestead sales tax (LHOST) on January 1, 2028. The bill also creates separate homestead sales taxes for schools (S-LHOST, up to 2 percent) and for cities (M-HOST, up to 1 percent), and adds a new excise tax on certain data centers to fund a Homeowner's Tax Relief Fund.

What remains is a single county-level LHOST of 1 percent starting in 2028. Existing LOST, HOST, EHOST and RHOST taxes would convert into the LHOST, FLOST could convert if local voters approve, and the local sales tax cap would rise to 5 percent, with these deadlines moved from mid-2027 to the end of 2027. New items include voter approval for city, county and school budgets that raise property tax revenue by more than 3 percent or inflation, limits on the dates for those special elections, a ban on back-billing homeowners for homestead exemptions applied by mistake through no fault of their own, a nonbinding November 2026 statewide vote on fully exempting homesteads from property tax, and a statement that future sales tax on data center computer equipment should fund homestead tax relief.

bills.headline: Reorganizes the state fire office, adds building permit appeals, and raises smoke detector fines.
bills.lastAction: Senate Agreed House Amend or Sub As Amended
bills.recap: This bill restructures the Safety Fire Commissioner's office, adds a deputy commissioner, and creates a new appeals board for local building permit rulings tied to fire safety standards. The board includes the state fire marshal, local officials, and licensed residential and commercial contractors, and it can overturn local stop-work orders that do not pose an imminent danger. It also lets the Commissioner order immediate evacuations of unsafe buildings, raises the fine for occupants who fail to maintain a working smoke detector from $25 to $100 per detector after a warning, and raises the manufactured home reinspection fee from $15 to $150. Realtors may care because builders gain a faster path to challenge permit holds, while homeowners, renters, and manufactured home makers face higher fees and fines. Much of the rest of the bill covers fireworks sales rules.

bills.headline: Broad code cleanup repeals unfunded, outdated, and unconstitutional Georgia laws.
bills.recap: HB 485 is a large housekeeping bill that repeals unfunded programs, updates outdated references, and removes or rewrites laws courts found unconstitutional. A few pieces touch real estate: it revises which covenant limits in Code Section 44-3-234 do not apply to property owners' association instruments, repeals a subparagraph in the property tax definitions, and simplifies a rule on loan fees paid to third parties. It also rewrites the law letting counties and cities levy occupation taxes on businesses and professionals, which can include real estate brokerages. Most changes are technical, so day-to-day impact for Realtors should be small, but HOA and local business tax details are worth noting.

bills.headline: Revises city deannexation rules and requires county consent for certain annexations.
bills.recap: The bill requires cities to report deannexations to the state and the county the same way they already report annexations. It sets a new county-consent rule for annexations in certain counties, such as a county with an unincorporated county seat that runs its own broadband utility and borders a large military base. For deannexations requested by all owners, it caps each action at ten parcels and requires the county to consent. If the county consents, the city must approve unless it finds harm to health, safety, and welfare, with a 90-day deadline when the county owns all the parcels. Realtors may care because city or county status affects a property's taxes, services, and zoning rules.

bills.headline: Extends state sales tax break on materials for charity-built affordable homes.
bills.recap: This bill changes an existing state sales tax exemption for building materials bought by 501(c)(3) charities to build, renovate, or rehab affordable single-family homes. The homes must be sold to first-time buyers earning 80% or less of area median income, with zero-interest loans from the charity. Buyers must live in the home, and a 30-year resale covenant limits future sales to buyers under the same income cap. The bill removes the December 31, 2031 end date, making the break permanent starting January 1, 2027, which could lower costs for groups like Habitat-style builders and add entry-level homes.

bills.headline: Lets counties adopt a 1% sales tax to fund extra homestead property tax relief.
bills.recap: The Senate substitute creates an 'alternative homestead option sales tax' of 1% that counties can adopt only if voters approve both the tax and a matching local homestead exemption. Up to 25% of the money can go to capital projects, which for counties means roads only. Most of the rest funds a homestead exemption on primary homes and up to five acres, which can cover up to 100% of county property taxes. Leftover funds roll back the county millage rate, and the tax and exemption end after ten years unless renewed. Realtors may care because lower county tax bills can reduce ownership costs and change how listings compare across counties.

bills.headline: Requires home sellers to disclose known flood damage, claims, and repairs in writing.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, sellers of one-to-four family homes in Georgia must state in writing whether, during their ownership, the property had flood damage, flood insurance claims, flood repairs, repetitive loss notices, or notices requiring flood insurance. Sellers must give approximate flood dates and describe repairs, and willful omissions count as a violation of the Fair Business Practices Act. Sellers and brokers do not have to investigate beyond what the seller knows. The bill also sets a $1,500 fine, plus attorney's fees or court costs, for each mechanic lien filed in bad faith or without real justification.

bills.headline: Replaces Georgia's base-year homestead exemption with a mandatory exemption phasing up to 50%.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: This House substitute changes the statewide homestead exemption from a cap on assessment increases to a flat cut in taxable home value. The cut starts at 10% in 2027 and rises to 50% by 2031. It applies to all counties and cities with no opt-out, but no longer applies to school taxes. It also lets local sales taxes total up to 5% to replace lost revenue, with FLOST adoptable by resolution instead of a vote. Local budgets that raise property tax revenue by more than 3% or inflation, whichever is greater, would need voter approval or a local act of the General Assembly. The exemption does not transfer to a new owner, and the bill adds a November 2026 advisory vote on fully eliminating homeowner property taxes. Realtors should note the big cut in owner-occupied tax bills and the higher sales taxes that may come with it.

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee's version keeps the original changes: it makes the statewide base year homestead exemption mandatory and removes the homestead exemption condition for calling a special district sales tax (FLOST) vote. It adds a new section on how that sales tax money lowers property taxes. Each year, the local roll-back rate must be cut by the millage equal to the net sales tax money received in the prior tax year or through June 30 of the current year. Tax bills must still show how much property tax was reduced, and the state commissioner cannot certify a local tax digest if the money is not used only for tax relief.

versions.name: Engrossed

versions.changes: The House Ways & Means substitute turns a short Senate bill into a broad property tax overhaul called the "Homeownership Opportunity and Market Equalization Act of 2026." It still makes the statewide base-year homestead exemption mandatory, but it no longer applies where a local base-year or adjusted base-year homestead exemption is already in effect. Starting January 1, 2028, the LOST, HOST, EHOST, and RHOST sales taxes convert into a new 1% Local Homestead Option Sales Tax (LHOST) for homestead property tax relief, FLOST can be adopted by resolution instead of a referendum, and the local sales tax cap becomes 5%. Starting 2028, local governments and school boards that raise property tax revenue by more than 3% or inflation (not counting growth) need voter approval or a local Act of the General Assembly, and votes on revenue increases are limited to certain election dates. For homeowners, the bill sets a 50% penalty for failing to report losing homestead eligibility, bars back-billing for homestead mistakes that were not the owner's fault, adds a statewide homestead database, and ends the estimated roll-back rate shown on assessment notices.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new House committee version drops the plan to convert local sales taxes (LOST, HOST, EHOST, RHOST) into a new Local Homestead Option Sales Tax. It also drops the higher school reserve cap, the limits on special election dates, the homestead penalty and statewide database rules, and the ban on billing owners for back taxes when a homestead exemption was applied by mistake. Instead, the statewide homestead exemption changes from a base-year (value freeze) exemption to a flat cut in the home's taxable value. That cut is 10% in 2027 and rises 10 points a year to 50% in 2031. The exemption no longer applies to school taxes and becomes mandatory, though the bill still contains opt-out wording from current law. Other changes: the 5% local sales tax cap and the 3% revenue limits on local budgets now start in 2027 instead of 2028, and FLOST money can cover losses from the homestead exemption. Sales tax returns must also show where the tax was collected. The bill adds a nonbinding November 2026 statewide ballot question on full property tax relief for homeowners and states an intent to use certain data center equipment sales tax, starting in 2029, for homestead tax relief grants.

bills.headline: Creates a fast sheriff process for owners to remove squatters and tightens squatting penalties.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: This House substitute, called the Georgia Anti-Squatting Act of 2026, replaces the original bill's limits on large corporate home ownership. It lets a property owner or their authorized agent file a sworn complaint with the sheriff or another certified officer to have squatters removed quickly, without a full eviction case, if conditions are met: no lease, no family tie, and no pending lawsuit. Showing a fake lease or deed to stay in a property becomes a felony with at least one year in prison, and convicted squatters must pay the owner back based on fair market rent. The bill also gives innkeepers faster removal of guests whose stays have ended and lets landlords use off-duty officers if a writ of possession is not carried out within 7 days instead of 14. Owners who wrongly use the process can owe damages and attorney's fees. Realtors handling vacant listings or investor properties should know this new tool exists.

It adds new tax penalties. Businesses over the 500-home limit, not counting homes they built, would lose certain Georgia tax credits, including the housing tax credit. They would also lose some depreciation deductions (Section 179) and some investment expense deductions on those homes. Brokers working with business clients who are buying or leasing homes must also tell those clients in a timely way that they may lose these tax credits.

All of the Senate-passed version is gone: the 500-home limit on companies, the ban on foreign investment vehicles owning rental homes, the related tax credit and depreciation limits, and the broker disclosure duty. The new bill is the "Georgia Anti-Squatting Act of 2026." It lets owners or their agents file a sworn complaint so law enforcement can quickly remove squatters, and it makes showing a fake lease or deed to stay on a property a felony with at least one year in prison. It also lets magistrate courts hear squatting cases anywhere in the county and gives hotels a faster way to remove guests whose stay has ended. It shortens the wait from 14 to 7 days before a landlord can hire off-duty officers to carry out an eviction, and it takes effect when signed.

bills.recap: This bill would require state Department of Community Affairs home buying programs, like Georgia Dream, to offer a $30,000 down payment loan and a $15,000 closing cost loan. The loans would carry zero interest, with 10% forgiven each year and any balance forgiven after ten years of living in the home. Income limits would rise to 140% of area median income in high-cost counties, and at least 20% of funds would be set aside for first-generation buyers and full-time public service workers like teachers, police, firefighters, EMTs, and healthcare workers. Realtors may see more qualified first-time buyers who can cover upfront costs in pricier markets.

bills.headline: Lets landowners merge multiple conservation-use tax covenants into one new ten-year covenant.
bills.recap: This bill lets a single owner with several parcels under separate conservation-use tax covenants combine them into one new ten-year covenant without breaking the old ones. Parcels with delinquent taxes can't be combined, and the owner must file a property tax return by the normal deadline. It also allows carbon sequestration as a secondary use on conservation land, and gives a new qualified owner 180 days after buying covenant land to switch it to a forest land covenant without penalty. Realtors who sell rural, farm, or timber land should note these changes, which apply starting with the 2027 tax year.

bills.headline: Raises condo owner deductible cap to $25,000 and updates foreclosure, title, and judge privacy rules.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: This bill, called the Real Estate Security and Title Act, raises the most a condo association can charge one unit owner toward the master policy insurance deductible from $5,000 to $25,000 per loss. Associations must also notify owners in writing of any big change in the master policy deductible. The bill lets the lender foreclosing on a property make a credit bid at a judicial sale instead of paying cash, and it sets stricter experience rules for special masters in some quiet title cases. It also expands privacy protections that hide judges' and their spouses' home addresses and parcel numbers in public records, while still letting title insurers and their attorneys get full copies for title work, so Realtors may want to remind condo buyers and owners to check their HO-6 coverage.

bills.headline: Bans taxpayer phone numbers from public and sold property tax records.
bills.recap: This bill bars anyone from including taxpayer phone numbers in tax rolls, assessment records, or other public property tax documents. The ban covers paper and electronic records, including bulk data sales, open records requests, and third-party agreements. Reckless or knowing disclosure can bring a civil penalty of up to $5,000 and counts as a violation of the Fair Business Practices Act, with exceptions for internal government use, court orders, and written taxpayer consent. Realtors and data vendors who rely on tax record data for owner outreach would lose access to phone numbers from this source.

bills.headline: Requires foreclosure notices to explain how homeowners can claim surplus sale funds.
bills.recap: Lenders must already send homeowners a written foreclosure notice at least 30 days before a sale. This bill adds that the notice must tell the homeowner they can claim any surplus money left after the sale pays off the mortgage and other liens, and explain how to make that claim. It must also warn, in bold, that unclaimed surplus funds may go to the state as abandoned property after the legal time limit, currently five years. Realtors working with distressed sellers may find this helpful, since it makes clear that money can remain after a foreclosure sale.

bills.headline: Cuts or eliminates Gwinnett school property taxes on homes owned by seniors 65 and older.
bills.recap: This local bill gives Gwinnett County senior homeowners aged 65 to 69 a 50 percent exemption from school district property taxes on their home. Seniors 70 and older would be fully exempt from school taxes on their home. To qualify, owners must have had a homestead exemption in the district for five of the last six years, and the exemption covers up to five acres. It needs a local voter referendum in November 2026 and would start in 2027, which could encourage seniors to stay in their homes and affect move-up inventory.

Every sales contract for land or homes in a district must carry a bold disclosure warning buyers about these added costs, so agents will need to spot and explain them. It only takes effect January 1, 2027, if voters approve a related constitutional amendment in November 2026.

bills.headline: Speeds building permits with online status tracking and wider use of private reviewers.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, cities and counties that issued more than 250 building permits the prior year must run a free public website showing real-time permit status, missed deadlines, and reasons for denials. Builders could hire licensed private engineers, architects, or qualified inspectors for plan reviews and inspections at any time, with local permit fees cut by 50 percent. Inspection reports from private providers would count as approved unless the local government flags problems within five business days. For erosion and land-disturbance permits, local officials must publish a list of required materials, decide on completeness within five days, and give written, specific reasons for any denial. Realtors may care because faster, more transparent permitting could shorten new-construction timelines and help buyers and sellers track projects.

The bill also widens the use of private engineers, architects, and inspectors for plan reviews and inspections, including erosion control work, and cuts local permit fees by 50 percent when an applicant uses one. bills.recap: This proposed change to the Georgia Constitution would let any owner in a condo, HOA community, or similar shared-ownership development go to court to stop someone from occupying another home there without permission. Today, usually only the owner of the affected property can bring that kind of case. If the legislature passes it, voters would decide on the statewide ballot. Realtors may care because it gives neighbors a new tool against squatters, which could help protect property values and the appeal of homes in these communities.

bills.headline: Lets condo and HOA neighbors seek removal of squatters from nearby homes.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: This bill expands Georgia's squatter removal process. It lets other owners in the same condo or HOA community file a sworn statement asking law enforcement to remove someone living in a unit or lot without a right to be there. The neighbor must first send the owner three days' written notice by certified mail or overnight delivery, and the owner can block the action; the association must help with notice. The person in the home gets three days to file a counter-statement claiming a legal right, which sends the case to magistrate court. Realtors with vacant listings or clients in condo and HOA communities may see faster squatter removals starting July 1, 2026.

bills.headline: Proposes constitutional amendment letting local governments tax data centers differently to ease other property taxes.
bills.recap: This resolution asks voters to amend the Georgia Constitution so lawmakers can treat data center property as its own tax class. Counties, cities, and school systems could then tax data centers at different rates or values. The stated goal is to reduce the property tax burden on other property, which could include homes. Realtors may care because it could affect local property tax bills and the cost of owning a home in areas with data centers.

bills.headline: Doubles conservation land donation tax credits and extends the program through 2031.
bills.recap: This bill expands Georgia's income tax credit for donating land or conservation easements. The credit rises from 25% to 50% of the land's value, with the per-donation cap going from $500,000 to $1 million. Yearly caps per taxpayer also double. The statewide total rises from $4 million to $30 million per year from mid-2026 through 2031, and new applications will be accepted until the end of 2031. The State Properties Commission's appraisal review role and the special penalty on appraisers for inflated values are repealed. Instead, the Department of Natural Resources reviews appraisals and reports overvalued ones to the Georgia Real Estate Commission for possible discipline. Realtors working with rural, farm or timber landowners should know that conservation easements limit subdividing, building and mining on the land, but the bigger credit may make them more attractive.

bills.headline: Reorganizes the state fire safety office and adds permit appeals, evacuation powers, and higher fines.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: This bill updates Georgia's Safety Fire Commissioner's office, adding a deputy commissioner and new enforcement powers. It creates a seven-member appeals board that can review local building permit rulings based on fire safety standards, and can overrule local stop-work orders that pose no imminent danger. The Commissioner could order immediate evacuation of any building with an imminent life safety hazard, even if it has a certificate of occupancy. It also raises the fine for an occupant who fails to maintain a smoke detector from $25 to $100 per detector, after a first warning, and raises the manufactured home reinspection fee from $15 to $150.

bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: This bill sets up a new class of remote online notaries in Georgia, starting January 1, 2027, who can notarize documents by live video. Real estate documents, including deeds, could be signed electronically and witnessed by video, and clerks may record them once both witness signatures and seals are present. A Georgia attorney must still supervise real estate closings. Knowingly recording a one-to-four family home document that came from the unauthorized practice of law would become an unfair business practice. For Realtors, this could make closings easier for out-of-town or overseas buyers and sellers, with remote notary fees capped at $25.

bills.headline: Updates Georgia transfer-on-death deed rules for acceptance, revocation, liens, and estates.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: This bill rewrites Georgia's transfer-on-death deed rules, which let owners name who gets their property at death. Each beneficiary must sign and record an affidavit, including the deed book and page, to take ownership. Revocation now needs only one witness plus an officer, and selling the property or putting it in the owner's trust automatically revokes the deed. Estates can pay a property's mortgage, taxes, and urgent repairs and get a lien for repayment, and they can sell property from an insolvent estate facing foreclosure if no beneficiary has accepted. Realtors handling inherited property should watch for these new title, lien, and recording steps.

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

bills.title: Property; transfer-on-death deeds; modify certain provisions

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee rewrote HB 899. Agents acting under a power of attorney can no longer sign transfer-on-death deeds at all, and the death certificate access rule for beneficiaries moves into the vital records law. Title still passes only after a beneficiary signs and records the acceptance affidavit within nine months, and that affidavit must now list the deed book and page. A beneficiary who dies after the owner but before accepting loses their share, which is split among the living beneficiaries. The deed now wins over the estate's unsecured debts rather than a year's support petition, and the one-person-accepts-for-all grace period moves to July 1, 2026. The estate must give beneficiaries notice of the deed. A solvent estate can pay the mortgage, taxes and urgent repairs and then claim a special lien. That lien ranks below tax liens and earlier security deeds, and it must be filed, mailed and foreclosed like a mechanic's lien. An insolvent estate facing foreclosure can record a notice and sell the home if no beneficiary has accepted.

bills.headline: Constitutional amendment would cut homestead taxable value from 40% to 10% over ten years.
bills.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would lower the taxable value of homestead properties from 40% to 10% of appraised value, dropping 3 points a year starting in 2027. Local governments could speed up the cut. To make up lost revenue, counties, cities and school systems could add a new local homestead option sales tax, up to 2% for schools and 1% for local governments. It also removes the $18,000 cap on the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment and adds a full homestead exemption for 100% disabled veterans who buy, build or inherit a primary home. It also caps school sales taxes at a combined 2%. For Realtors, this could greatly lower property tax bills for owner-occupants and change the cost of owning a home, but voters must approve it first.

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

bills.title: Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment clause; remove cap on benefits - CA

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The House Ways and Means Committee rewrote this proposed constitutional amendment. It still exempts all homestead properties from local and school property taxes by January 1, 2032, with optional local sales taxes to make up the lost revenue. The new version adds that homes may still be taxed to pay off existing local bond debt. If voters reject a required sales tax referendum after 2037, local governments could tax homesteads again. The new local finance assessments are no longer tied to each parcel of real property, and unpaid assessments would no longer become a lien on the property. Instead, the state could let local governments temporarily suspend the owner's homestead exemptions or use other ways to collect. Property tax rollbacks would only be required for assessments that pay for services, not for capital projects. Both the school and local government millage referendum rules would now apply to increases in property tax revenue, and the law would have to account for inflation and growth. The ballot question now promises "100 percent" instead of "complete" property tax relief.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new substitute drops the plan to fully exempt all homesteads from local property taxes by 2032. Instead, it would lower the taxable value of homesteads from 40 percent of appraised value to 10 percent, cutting it by 3 percent each year starting in 2027, and local governments could speed this up. It also drops voter approval of millage increases and the new local finance assessments, and cuts the local homestead sales tax cap for cities and counties from 3 percent to 1 percent. If a later referendum on that sales tax fails, homesteads go back to 40 percent. New pieces include a full homestead exemption for 100 percent disabled veterans who build, buy, or inherit a home, and letting the state use dedicated money, such as sales tax from data centers, to fund homeowner tax relief grants.

versions.changes: The House Rules Committee replaced the Ways and Means version with its own. The new version adds a rule for local governments that don't assess homes at 40 percent of value: they must cut their assessment rate by a total of 75 percent over 10 years, in equal steps starting in 2027. It also lets the state give grants to local governments and school systems to replace money lost from lower home assessments. The local homestead sales tax is now tied directly to making up that lost revenue, with the 1 percent local government share split based on each government's loss. The ballot question now mentions the 10-year phase-in and the goal of offsetting lost property tax revenue.

bills.headline: Lets counties tax large single-family rental owners' homes at full value, not 40 percent.
bills.recap: Georgia normally taxes property at 40 percent of its fair market value. This bill says single-family rental homes owned by larger investors may be taxed at 100 percent of value. Homes owned by "community housing providers" stay at the normal 40 percent rate. That group covers individuals, nonprofits, charities, and S corporations, LLCs, or partnerships owning 500 or fewer properties in Georgia. Larger rental owners would have to give tax assessors income data on request. Assessors could also ask smaller owners for a sworn affidavit by April 1. Realtors working with institutional investors or rental buyers should watch how this could change holding costs and investor demand.

bills.headline: Creates a state towed-vehicle database and tightens notice rules for towing companies.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: The bill has the Department of Revenue set up an online database by January 1, 2027, where owners can look up a towed car by VIN or plate. Towing firms must enter towed vehicles within three days and send owner notices within seven days instead of 15. Starting in 2028, owners get 30 days instead of 10 to answer a lien petition, and firms that skip notice steps lose storage fees. Realtors may care because property owners, landlords, and HOAs who have cars towed from their lots are covered by these rules.

bills.headline: Revises local sales tax rules, school construction refunds, and LOST revenue sharing.
bills.recap: This bill gives school systems a refund of local sales taxes paid on construction materials for SPLOST-funded school projects. The refund applies only where the school system has a homestead exemption that freezes or limits home value increases for all residents, and it ends in 2033. It also tightens the 2% cap on local sales taxes, updates rules for a special sales tax used for property tax relief, and changes how counties and cities split LOST money when one side won't sign the deal. Realtors may care because these changes push local governments toward homestead value freezes and affect sales tax money used to hold down property taxes.

bills.headline: Bars Georgia governments from using international designations to restrict private property use.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: This bill, the Georgia Land Sovereignty and Private Property Protection Act, says designations from groups like the United Nations, UNESCO, or the World Health Organization have no legal effect in Georgia unless state law allows it. State agencies and local governments could not use them in zoning, permitting, land use planning, or environmental review. If such reliance lowers a property's market value or use, it would count as a taking that requires just compensation. Affected owners could sue for court orders and recover attorney's fees, which may matter to Realtors working with land or development deals.

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The committee rewrote the bill. It no longer simply declares that the UN and World Health Organization have no power in Georgia. It is now the 'Georgia Land Sovereignty and Private Property Protection Act,' focused on land use and private property. Under the new version, designations or guidance from international groups (such as the UN, UNESCO, or WHO) have no legal effect unless the legislature passes a law allowing it. State agencies and local governments could not rely on these designations for zoning, permits, land use planning, or environmental review. Money collected from high-tech data centers and the insurance premium tax could fund refundable state income tax credits for people living in 'qualifying homes,' which lawmakers would define later. It also raises the cap on the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment from the equivalent of an $18,000 homestead exemption to $150,000, and lets local governments and school systems fund their own adjustments. For Realtors, this could mean lower yearly costs for homeowners with a homestead exemption, which may help affordability and owner appeal.

bills.headline: Lets local voters create programs that give homesteads property tax credits from surplus funds.
bills.recap: This bill lets Georgia counties and cities set up local homeowner's incentive adjustment grant programs, but only if local voters approve them in a referendum. When a local government collects more revenue than it budgeted, it can put the extra money into a special fund and use it to give tax credits to homes with a homestead exemption. The credit shows up on the tax bill and cannot exceed what the owner owes. The bill takes effect January 1, 2027, only if voters ratify a constitutional amendment removing the $18,000 assessed value cap. Realtors may care because lower tax bills on homesteads can make owning a home more affordable and may come up with buyers comparing areas.

bills.headline: Shields businesses that use, receive or dispose of PFAS chemicals from most lawsuits.
bills.recap: This bill gives legal immunity to 'PFAS receivers,' meaning businesses, farms, landfills, wastewater plants and others that use, buy, own or dispose of products containing PFAS 'forever chemicals.' Chemical makers are not covered. Receivers can only be sued if a plaintiff shows gross negligence, and those that met all EPA and state testing limits are fully protected. Personal injury and death claims, state enforcement, and duties to warn the public still apply. Realtors may care because owners of land or homes harmed by PFAS pollution could find it harder to recover money for property damage or lost value.

versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee version narrows the lawsuit shield for people and businesses that use, buy, own or dispose of products with PFAS ("forever chemicals"). The protection no longer covers gross negligence, and the bill now defines that term. A person suing must spell out specific facts showing gross negligence, and a judge decides whether those facts are enough. Waste handlers are covered only if they are licensed and regulated by the state Environmental Protection Division. A separate protection now covers sending PFAS waste to wastewater plants and public landfills, but only when the receiver met all federal and state testing rules and limits. The shield now also covers environmental engineers and consultants who work for these receivers. State Environmental Protection Division enforcement claims are still not blocked, and the January 2024 date limit on those claims was removed. The bill also states that it does not limit claims for personal injury or death, or any duty to warn the public of safety threats.

bills.headline: Requires HOAs and condo associations to share key records with homeowners.
bills.recap: This bill creates the Right to Information for Homeowners Act. HOAs, condo and property owners' associations would have to provide documents like budgets, bank statements, insurance policies, bylaws and meeting minutes within 14 days of a request. They would also need a secure online database, an annual report on finances and reserves, an independent audit every two years, and seven years of bank records. Owners could sue for damages, and associations could be fined up to $500 per violation. Realtors may find it easier to get association records that buyers and sellers need when weighing a home in a community association.

bills.headline: Requires landlords to show total rental price and bans hidden rental fees.
bills.recap: HB1188 would make it an unfair business practice under Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act for a landlord to sign a lease or take payment before clearly showing the total rental price, including mandatory and government fees but not utilities. It also bans hidden fees, such as fees above actual cost, fees for services not provided or legally required, fees tied to required vendors, and fees not written in the lease. The rules cover apartments and homes as well as hotels, vacation rentals, and other short-term rentals. Agents and brokers who handle leasing or property management should review fee practices and listing price displays, since the law would apply to leases, renewals, and extensions signed after it takes effect.

bills.headline: Requires rental homes to be habitable and gives tenants remedies like rent withholding.
bills.recap: Every residential lease would include a promise, which cannot be waived, that the home is fit to live in. Landlords would have to follow health and safety codes, keep common areas safe, and maintain plumbing, electrical, heating and AC, and appliances. They would also have to handle trash removal and supply running water, hot water and reasonable heat. If a serious problem is not fixed within one week of notice, tenants could end the lease, withhold rent, sue for damages, or make repairs and deduct the cost from rent. Agents who manage rentals or work with investors should expect stricter repair duties and new tenant leverage, while tenants must still keep units clean and avoid damage.

bills.recap: This bill expands Georgia's existing early lease termination law, which now covers family violence and stalking orders, to include tenants or legal occupants who were victims of firearm violence at or near their rental home. The tenant gives the landlord written notice, and the lease ends 30 days later. The notice must include proof, such as a police record, medical record, a letter from a victim services provider, or a sworn statement from a qualified person like a counselor or clergy member. bills.headline: Limits HOA and condo foreclosures and creates a state ombudsman for community associations.
bills.recap: This bill limits when HOAs and condo associations can foreclose on a home over unpaid dues. They could not foreclose over fines alone, or for less than $2,000 or less than a year of assessments, and the association and its board members could not buy the home at the sale. Owners would get 180 days after a foreclosure sale to buy the home back, and newer associations would have to waive dues for at least 12 months for owners who become disabled with financial hardship or who die with an insolvent estate. It also creates a state Community Association Ombudsman to handle complaints and monitor board elections, paid for by an annual $25-per-unit registration fee on associations. Realtors should note the added protections for owners in HOA and condo communities, possible fee pass-throughs to owners, and the 180-day buyback period on HOA foreclosure sales.

bills.headline: Lets judges and their spouses ask governments to hide their home addresses and property records.
bills.recap: This law lets current and former judges and their spouses ask state and local agencies to keep their home address, personal phone number, and property or tax records out of public view. They use a statewide form from the Administrative Office of the Courts, and agencies must comply within 30 days of a valid request. Covered offices include county clerk's offices and boards of tax assessors, and it replaces the old state database system. Realtors may find some property and tax records restricted when researching ownership or comparing properties owned by judges.

bills.headline: Updates rules on convenience fees for paying certain loans electronically.
bills.recap: This law lets lenders and merchants charge a nonrefundable fee when people pay electronically, such as by card or electronic transfer. The fee can equal the actual processing cost, the average cost for that payment type, or up to $5, whichever is greater. A fee-free payment option must also be offered, and the fee must be clearly disclosed in advance. It applies to certain consumer loans, installment loans, retail and home solicitation sales contracts, car financing, and insurance premium finance, not to standard home mortgages.

Realtors with rental property or their own businesses may see state and federal tax treatment continue to differ on items like depreciation.

Realtors handling estate or trust-owned property may see clearer rules on who has authority to sign and sell, and more electronic paperwork.

bills.recap: This law updates Georgia's solid waste rules for landfills and other waste facilities, starting January 1, 2026. Permit applicants must submit written proof from the local government, no more than 36 months old, that the site meets local zoning and the local waste plan. It also removes some older limits, including a ban on certain landfills taking outside waste in groundwater recharge areas. Realtors may care because new or expanded landfills nearby can affect property values and buyer interest.

bills.headline: Creates tax-free catastrophe savings accounts for homeowners' storm deductibles and uninsured repairs.
bills.recap: Starting with tax year 2026, Georgia homeowners can open one catastrophe savings account per primary residence. They can deduct contributions from state income tax, and interest earned is tax-free. The money can be used for their homeowner's insurance deductible or uninsured repair costs after a disaster declared by the Governor. Contribution limits depend on the deductible: up to $2,000 for deductibles of $1,000 or less, up to twice the deductible (max $25,000) for higher ones, and up to $250,000 for self-insured owners, capped at the home's value. Withdrawals for other uses are taxed as income. Realtors may find this a useful point for buyers worried about high deductibles and storm risk.

bills.headline: Updates GDOT hearing notices, condo/HOA common property buys, truck towing, and utility relocation costs.
bills.recap: This law lets the Georgia Department of Transportation post public hearing notices online and in print, including on its website. It also lets GDOT negotiate with a condo or HOA board to buy common property for road projects, and the board can sign on behalf of all owners unless the recorded documents say otherwise. If talks fail, GDOT can sue the association instead of each owner, and owners are bound by the result, though owners hit harder than others must be named individually. Any money paid is split among owners based on their ownership shares, which Realtors working with condo and HOA buyers or sellers near road projects should know.

bills.recap: Under this law, only the homeowner, not every lienholder, must sign and file the Certificate of Permanent Location that turns a manufactured home into real property. A lender who held a lien on the home before the conversion keeps its personal property rights and priority until the loan is paid off. That lender can repossess and remove the home without the landowner's or mortgage holder's consent, and it or a buyer from it can get a new title. Realtors listing or selling land with a converted manufactured home should check for unpaid prior liens on the home itself, since they can survive the conversion; the law applies to contracts made on or after July 1, 2025.

Owners 65 to 69 get the greater of 50% or $60,000 of assessed value exempt, and owners 70 to 76 get the greater of 75% or $80,000 exempt. Owners 77 and older get a full exemption on homes worth up to $500,000, with total exemptions capped at $150 million in 2026. Voters had to approve it in November 2025 for it to start January 1, 2026, and Realtors may find it affects older owners' decisions to stay in or sell their homes.

bills.headline: Freezes Clayton County tax values for seniors, disabled veterans, and other qualifying homeowners.
bills.recap: This law creates a Clayton County homestead exemption that blocks county property tax increases from rising assessed values. It covers seniors, disabled veterans, 100 percent disabled residents, and unremarried surviving spouses of peace officers or firefighters killed in the line of duty. The taxable value is held at a base year and can rise only by inflation or by major improvements. It does not cover school, city, state, or bond debt taxes. It runs from 2026 through 2030 only if voters approved it in November 2025. The exemption does not transfer to a buyer, so agents should warn buyers that taxes may jump after purchase.

bills.headline: Updates Georgia banking law and adds new financial and oversight rules for mortgage companies.
bills.recap: This broad banking update sets minimum net worth for mortgage brokers ($50,000) and lenders ($100,000 plus $1 million in liquidity), and requires mortgage companies to have boards, risk programs and internal audits. It replaces a flat felony ban with a seven-year lookback, except for listed financial crimes like fraud and theft, which still bar a license at any time. It also requires annual external audits for mortgage lenders, lets regulators withdraw incomplete license applications after 30 days, and makes changes for credit unions, check cashers, money transmitters, installment lenders and foreign banks. Realtors may care because smaller mortgage shops face higher costs and paperwork, which could affect which lenders their clients can use.

bills.headline: Lets certain farm businesses lease conservation use land without losing the tax break.
bills.recap: Under current law, land in Georgia's conservation use program loses its lower property tax assessment if it is leased to someone who could not qualify for the program themselves. This bill exempts certain registered businesses from that rule. A business qualifies if it is owned only by U.S. citizens, mainly produces farm or timber products, and earns at least 80 percent of its income from conservation uses in Georgia, or if a member owns at least 25 percent of the leased land and would qualify. The bill also renews a state tax credit for film postproduction companies through 2030, which does not involve real estate. The changes apply to tax years starting January 1, 2026, which matters for Realtors who work with rural land buyers, sellers, and investors.

bills.headline: Out-of-state landlords of houses and duplexes must hire a licensed broker.
bills.recap: Landlords who live outside Georgia and own or run single-family or duplex rentals here must hire a licensed real estate broker. If that broker lives out of state, the broker must keep at least one person in Georgia to handle tenant maintenance requests and other issues. These landlords can no longer rely on the owner and full-time employee exemptions from broker licensing. The bill also says that when a code officer has probable cause of a violation at a broker-managed rental, the tenant must give the property manager's name, license number, and contact information on request. Realtors and property managers may see new business from out-of-state investors, along with closer code enforcement attention.

bills.recap: This law gives Fulton County School District homeowners age 65 or older a homestead exemption of 25% of their home's assessed value on school taxes. To qualify, a senior must own and live in the home and must have had a homestead exemption in the district for five of the last six years. The exemption covers up to five acres. Seniors must apply once with the Fulton County tax commissioner, and it renews automatically. It does not apply to state, county, city, or independent school district taxes, such as Atlanta's. It needed voter approval in November 2025 and would apply starting in 2026. Realtors may care because it lowers the cost of staying put for older Fulton owners. The five-of-six-years rule also means a senior who moves to a new home in the district may need time to qualify again.

bills.recap: When a buyer applies for a mortgage, credit bureaus can sell that inquiry as a "trigger lead" to other lenders. Under this law, lenders and brokers using those leads must say up front that they are not tied to the buyer's original lender. They must make a firm offer of credit and honor opt-outs and the do-not-call list. They also cannot quote rates or terms they know will later change for the worse. Violations count as unfair business practices and can lead to action against a lender's license. Realtors may see fewer confusing calls to their buyers during a deal, which may help keep closings on track. It took effect when signed.

versions.changes: The Senate committee kept the House version's changes to how arbitrators are picked and paid in city-county annexation disputes, and added a large new section on local zoning rules. The new section lets superior court rulings on zoning decisions be appealed directly to Georgia's higher courts. It also limits who local governments can hand zoning power to, and moves special use permits and variances tied to rezonings into the definition of a zoning decision. It changes notice timing as well: 15 to 45 days before quasi-judicial hearings (was 30 to 45), and 15 to 45 days between the two votes needed to allow multifamily uses in single-family zones (was at least 21 days). The zoning changes would take effect July 1, 2025, while the annexation arbitration changes still start January 1, 2026.

versions.changes: This version, as adopted by the full Senate, keeps the earlier committee changes and adds one new section. The new part changes the 'contiguous area' rule for annexing land that a city already owns. If the county governing board approves by resolution and a majority of county voters approve in a referendum, the city-owned land can still count as touching the city even if it is separated by other city or government land, state land, streets, creeks, rivers, or railroad or utility rights of way. This new part would take effect July 1, 2025; the rest of the bill, covering annexation arbitration panels and zoning appeals, is unchanged.

The final version also changes the rule for annexing city-owned land: county approval is still needed, but a countywide referendum is now required only when the land connects to the city across a street, waterway, or railroad or utility right of way, not for every such annexation. bills.headline: Creates a state trust fund to help buy and protect Georgia battlefield land.
bills.recap: This law creates the Vince Dooley Battlefield Trust Fund, run by the Department of Natural Resources, to give matching grants to nonprofits and state agencies that buy Georgia Civil War, Revolutionary War, or War of 1812 battlefield land or easements. Grants can cover up to 50 percent of appraised value plus closing costs like appraisals, surveys, and title insurance, and nonprofits must match each dollar. Every purchase must carry a perpetual conservation easement that restricts use or development. Realtors working near listed battlefields may see new nonprofit buyers for land, but those parcels would be permanently taken off the market for development.

bills.headline: Doubles the acreage cap for conservation use property tax breaks to 4,000 acres.
bills.recap: This law raises the maximum land one owner can enroll in Georgia's conservation use tax program from 2,000 to 4,000 acres. The program taxes qualifying farm, timber and environmentally sensitive land at its current use value instead of market value. It only takes effect January 1, 2027, if voters approve a matching constitutional amendment in November 2026; otherwise it is repealed. Realtors who sell large rural tracts should note that bigger landowners could see lower tax bills, and that conservation covenants and their rules can affect a land sale.

bills.headline: Raises the intangible recording tax threshold from three-year notes to 62-month notes.
bills.recap: Georgia charges an intangible recording tax on long-term notes secured by real estate. This law redefines a long-term note as one with any principal due more than 62 months out, instead of more than three years. Loans due within 62 months no longer owe the tax, and security deeds can simply state that fact instead of listing a due date. The same 62-month rule now applies to seller-financed sales using a bond for title, which can lower closing costs on short-term loans like bridge, construction, and seller-financed deals.

bills.headline: Lets the state licensing division director approve, renew, and reinstate professional licenses.
bills.recap: Starting July 1, 2026, the director of the Secretary of State's professional licensing boards division can approve, renew, or reinstate a license if the application clearly meets all requirements; unclear applications go to the licensing board. Licenses are valid for up to two years, with a 45-day grace period to renew after expiration if all requirements and fees are met. Board rules must be aimed at protecting public health, safety, and welfare, and the public roster will also list people issued cease and desist orders for working without a license. Realtors may care because faster licensing for building trades could speed up home repairs and construction, and the roster makes it easier to check whether a tradesperson is licensed.

bills.headline: Caps yearly school tax value increases on Cartersville homesteads at inflation, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Cartersville city school district taxes, so a home's taxable value for school taxes can only rise each year by the rate of inflation, plus the value of any major improvements. For homesteads first getting the break in 2026, the starting value is the 2024 assessed value, and current homestead holders get it automatically without a new application. The break needed approval from city school district voters in November 2025, and it would run from 2026 through 2030. It does not move to a new owner, so buyers start with a fresh base value, which matters when you explain tax bills to clients.

bills.recap: This new law lets local governments in Helene disaster counties waive timber harvest taxes on badly damaged timberland for late 2024 and all of 2025, with possible state grants to cover their lost revenue. It excludes certain Helene farm relief payments and 2025 crop insurance proceeds from state income tax. Through 2025, building materials used to repair greenhouses and animal barns are exempt from sales tax. Realtors who sell rural, farm, or timber land in south Georgia may see these benefits affect land values and owner decisions.

bills.recap: For one year after a natural disaster, contractors repairing disaster damage to a home commit an unfair practice if they fail to substantially start work within a year, do substandard work, ignore state building codes, or take an assignment of the homeowner's insurance money. Homeowners can cancel the contract until midnight on the fifth business day after their insurer says all or part of the claim is not covered, and contractors must give a boldface cancellation notice and form. The hold is waived for filings by attorneys, title insurance agents, licensed real estate licensees under Chapter 40 of Title 43, banks, mortgage lenders, servicers, surveyors, government officials, owners, or filers with a notarized affidavit or power of attorney. It also requires self-filers to record electronically starting January 1, 2026, when the law takes effect, so closings handled by professionals should not slow down, while property owners gain protection against deed theft.

Private parties could sue for $15,000 per property or actual damages, plus attorney's fees. The Attorney General or a district attorney could force a public sale of the extra properties. Companies over the cap could not lease those homes, and tenants could sue to get rent back. Lenders holding mortgages are exempt, and homes taken through foreclosure have two years to be sold. Brokers working for business buyers or landlords would have to tell those clients about these limits in a timely way.

bills.recap: If a landlord does not fix a major defect within 14 days of written notice, the tenant may hire a licensed professional to fix it. Agents who manage rentals or advise investors should note the new repair deadlines and possible rent reductions.

It also creates new exemptions for police, firefighters, and public EMTs disabled in the line of duty: 100% for total disability and 50% for partial disability. Voters must approve it statewide in November 2026, with an effective date of January 1, 2027, so Realtors working with these buyers should note the possible large tax savings that could affect affordability.

bills.recap: This local law lets the City of Cedartown use the powers in Georgia's Redevelopment Powers Law. That includes community redevelopment, creating tax allocation districts, and issuing tax allocation bonds. The powers only take effect if Cedartown voters approved them in a March 2025 referendum; otherwise the law repeals itself. Realtors working in Polk County may see new redevelopment projects and districts that affect land use, investment, and property values in parts of the city.

bills.recap: This bill, called the Okefenokee Protection Act, stops the state from issuing, changing, or renewing surface mining permits on Trail Ridge for applications filed on or after July 1, 2025. Trail Ridge is the raised land on the east side of the swamp that controls how it drains. It mainly affects mining companies and owners of land on Trail Ridge, whose land could no longer be sold or leased for new mining. Realtors in southeast Georgia may care because it changes land use options and possibly land values in that area.

bills.recap: This bill requires owners of facilities with a peak energy load of 30 megawatts or more, such as large data centers, to file yearly public reports with the state. Reports must cover energy and water use, water discharge, property taxes paid, air permits, and noise levels for properties within a quarter mile. Proposed facilities must file projections before seeking tax incentives or permits, and those that fail to file lose tax incentives. Realtors may find these public reports useful when advising clients about homes or land near large industrial sites.

bills.recap: Today, a Georgia city can annex land next to its borders when 100 percent of the landowners apply. This bill adds a new step: the county where the land sits must pass a resolution agreeing to the annexation. Without county consent, the annexation cannot go forward. Realtors may care because annexation affects zoning, property taxes, utilities, and services, and this change could slow or block owner-requested annexations tied to development projects.

bills.recap: The bill caps local sales taxes at 2 percent, with set exceptions for school, transportation, transit, and certain other local taxes. Taxes already in place that go over the cap can continue but cannot be renewed when they expire. It also revises the special district sales tax for property tax relief, which requires local governments to have a base year or adjusted base year homestead exemption to share in the money. Realtors may care because these rules shape how much property tax relief homeowners can get and how local governments fund themselves.
