bills.recap: This bill stops condo associations, property owners' associations and HOAs from banning or restricting solar devices on an owner's roof, even a shared roof the association maintains. Associations could not require a permit or fee for solar devices, and any conflicting rules would be void. If a shared roof needs repair, the owner who installed the solar device pays to remove and reinstall it. The rules apply only to association documents, covenants and rules adopted, renewed or changed on or after January 1, 2026, so agents should check when a community's documents were last updated.

It would affect people living in extended-stay hotels and other lodging, often as temporary or transitional housing. bills.headline: Requires disclaimers on AI-generated images, video and audio used in commerce.
bills.recap: Starting July 1, 2025, anyone sharing AI-generated videos, audio or still images to promote business would have to disclose that AI was used. Visual disclaimers must be in writing, in each language used, with text at least 30 percent of the picture height and shown for at least 30 percent of a video's length. Audio disclaimers must be spoken at the same volume and speed as the content. Each image or file missing a disclaimer counts as a separate violation under the Fair Business Practices Act, so agents using AI virtual staging, enhanced listing photos or AI voiceovers would need to label them.

It also requires the utility to give customers free access to their own meter usage data and share it with third parties they approve. Realtors may care because it could lower utility costs for buyers and renters without rooftop panels, and usage data could help show a home's energy costs.

The affidavit must list the address, confirm ownership, state there is no current rental agreement, and ask that any unlawful tenant be removed within one calendar day once the affidavit is confirmed. The affidavit can then be used as a basis to demand possession in eviction (dispossessory) cases. Utility long-range plans would also have to list renewable resources, and the Georgia Environmental Finance Authority could finance solar, wind, battery storage, and transmission projects. bills.headline: Creates a 20% builder tax credit for new homes sold for $200,000 or less.
bills.recap: Starting in 2026, taxpayers who build a new single-family home and sell it to an individual or related individuals for $200,000 or less could claim a Georgia income tax credit equal to 20% of their construction costs. Unused credits can be carried forward for five years, or sold or transferred once per year to other Georgia taxpayers, with notice to the Department of Revenue within 30 days. The goal is to encourage more lower-priced new construction. Realtors working with first-time or budget buyers and builders may see more entry-level new homes if the bill passes.
bills.title: Income tax; tax credit for certain expenses incurred by taxpayers that sell new construction homes to certain individuals for up to a certain price; provide

bills.headline: Creates a 6% Georgia income tax credit for clean energy and battery storage investments.
bills.recap: Starting in 2026, this bill gives a state income tax credit equal to 6% of investment in new zero-emission power facilities and energy storage in Georgia. Buildings and their structural parts do not count, and unused credits carry forward three years. Credits can be sold to other Georgia taxpayers for at least 60% of their value. Realtors may care because the credit could make solar and battery systems somewhat cheaper for property owners, though the bill does not mention homes directly.
bills.title: Clean Energy Investment Tax Credit Act; enact

bills.headline: Creates a Georgia income tax credit of 3 cents per kilowatt hour for clean electricity.
bills.recap: Starting with tax years in 2026, this bill gives a state income tax credit of 3 cents for each kilowatt hour of electricity made at a new zero-emission facility in Georgia. Facilities must be placed in service after July 1, 2025, and qualify for 10 years. Credits can be carried forward three years or sold to other Georgia taxpayers for at least 60 percent of their value. The bill does not single out homes, but its wording on metered power that is used or stored could reach smaller systems such as solar, which may matter to owners and buyers weighing energy upgrades.

bills.headline: Limits what Georgia notaries can do and bans misleading 'notario' advertising.
bills.recap: HB189 says a notary commission does not allow someone to give legal advice, draft legal documents, act as an immigration consultant, or make certified copies of public records or recorded documents. Non-attorney notaries cannot use the terms 'notario' or 'notario publico' and must post their fee schedule, including in any language they advertise in. Notaries also cannot hold onto a customer's original documents or sign false certificates, and some violations count as deceptive trade practices. Realtors may care because notaries are part of signing deeds and closing papers, and recorded deeds would need certified copies from official sources instead of notaries.
bills.title: Notaries public; limitations regarding certain notarial acts; provide

bills.headline: Lets hotels lien removed guest property and quickly eject guests whose stays end.
bills.recap: This bill lets innkeepers hold a lien on a guest's belongings removed from a room once the guest's signed stay period ends. It lets an innkeeper sign an affidavit, after which a sheriff or other officer must remove the person within five days. If officers cannot act in time, the innkeeper may hire off-duty officers. It also says guests staying day-to-day or week-to-week are presumed hotel guests, not tenants, no matter how long they stay. That matters for extended-stay properties, because those occupants would not get landlord-tenant eviction protections.

bills.headline: Bars condo associations and HOAs from retaliating against owners who raise concerns.
bills.recap: This bill bars condo associations and property owners' associations from punishing owners who complain, report problems to a court or agency, give feedback, or organize. Banned retaliation includes raising an owner's fees, cutting services, blocking use of the home or common areas, or suddenly starting collection or lien actions. If an owner raised a life, health, safety, or habitability concern and the association acted against them within three months, that is presumed retaliation, though association-wide fee increases and written agreements are exempt. An owner can use retaliation as a defense to a lien foreclosure and recover one month's fees plus $500, court costs, and attorney's fees, which matters to Realtors working with buyers and sellers in HOA and condo communities.

bills.headline: Lets abuse victims end leases or have landlords remove abusers, and bars discrimination.
bills.recap: HB188 lets a tenant protected by a family violence or stalking order end their own lease on 30 days' written notice, or ask the landlord to end only the abuser's lease on a shared unit, with at least 72 hours' posted notice to the abuser. Remaining joint tenants cannot be charged higher rent, extra deposits, or early-termination fees, and the leaving tenant owes only prorated and past-due rent. Landlords may not refuse to rent to, renew, or terminate someone because they are a victim or previously ended a lease for this reason, and victims can sue if they do. Property managers and leasing agents should update lease practices, since these rules cannot be waived and apply to leases signed or renewed after the law takes effect.

bills.headline: Creates a state income tax deduction for timber losses on damaged Georgia timberland.
bills.recap: HB151 lets taxpayers subtract casualty losses of timber from Georgia taxable income, based on how much up to 2,000 acres of timberland dropped in value. The deduction only covers losses above the owner's cost basis and above any insurance, disaster aid, grants or other relief received. S corporations, partnerships and LLCs can claim it only at the entity level, and total deductions statewide are capped at $347 million per year. Realtors who work with rural land and timberland owners may care because it could ease the financial hit after storm damage and affect decisions to hold or sell land.

bills.headline: Lets counties extend historic property tax breaks up to 12 more years for income properties.
bills.recap: Georgia lets owners of rehabilitated or landmark historic properties keep a lower property tax assessment for nine years. This bill lets the county government approve up to 12 more years of that lower assessment, but only for income-producing real property. Owners of historic rental buildings and commercial properties could see lower tax bills for longer if their county agrees. Realtors working with historic investment properties may find them more attractive to buyers and owners.

bills.headline: Bans hairstyle-based race discrimination in housing, schools, and jobs.
bills.recap: HB135 updates Georgia's fair housing law so that 'race' includes hair texture and protective hairstyles such as braids, locs, and twists. This means treating a buyer or renter differently because of these hairstyles could count as illegal race discrimination in housing. The bill also adds the same protections for students at state-funded schools and for workers, and it lets employees sue employers within one year. Realtors, brokers, landlords, and property managers should know that hairstyle-based treatment of clients could become a fair housing violation.

bills.headline: Creates a state-run guest worker program to fill Georgia labor shortages.
bills.recap: This bill tells the Georgia Labor Commissioner to set up a state guest worker program for industries with proven labor shortages. Employers would pay fees and provide wages, health insurance, workers' comp and travel costs, plus housing if federal law requires it, through employer, rental or public housing. The program only starts if the Attorney General finds it can lawfully run under state and federal law. Realtors may care because it could add renters and boost the construction workforce in some areas.

bills.headline: Requires GDOT public hearings for major local road projects it helps design or build.
bills.recap: This bill requires the Georgia Department of Transportation to hold public hearings on 'local transportation projects of significant impact.' These are projects where GDOT helps a county, city, or private party with consultation, design, or construction, no matter who pays. They include new roads, road extensions, or major intersection changes that did not already go through local zoning or approval notice. The bill also makes the 21-day minimum deadline for requesting a hearing mandatory. Realtors may care because these road changes can shape traffic, access, and property values near homes and land, and owners would get more notice and a chance to comment.

bills.headline: Sets new board, voting, and election rules for Georgia condo associations and HOAs.
bills.recap: The bill gives each condo unit or lot one vote and requires boards of at least three members who own and live in the community, with only one board member per home. Associations must hold board elections at least yearly, keep ballot scans, and file results with the Secretary of State, which certifies them and handles election challenges from owners. Associations that fail to show they have enough board members face administrative suspension, and annual meetings can proceed without a quorum. Realtors may care because these rules shape how HOA and condo communities are run, and investor or nonresident owners could no longer serve on boards.

bills.headline: Creates a state grant program to improve drinking water in low-income communities.
bills.recap: HB43 creates the Disadvantaged Community Drinking Water Assistance Program, run by the state Environmental Protection Division. It offers grants, if lawmakers fund it, to low-income areas whose drinking water has run short or become unsafe. Money can pay for well treatment, new wells, linking homes to public water systems, connection fees, and emergency water. Realtors may care because homes with dry or contaminated wells can be hard to sell or finance, and these grants could help fix that.

bills.headline: Requires the Catoosa County Board of Education to adopt a balanced budget.
bills.recap: This local bill requires the Catoosa County school board to pass a balanced budget each year that covers all required spending and debt payments. When the state fully funds the Quality Basic Education formula, the board may not dip into its reserves to balance the budget. That limit is lifted during declared emergencies or when revenue falls short for reasons outside the district's control. Since school spending is mostly paid for with property taxes, Realtors may watch how this shapes future school tax rates and homeowner costs in Catoosa County.

bills.headline: Bans certain toxic flame retardant chemicals in carpet, furniture, bedding, and window treatments.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2026, manufacturers and retailers could not sell new carpet and padding, blinds and curtains, bedding, home upholstered furniture, or children's products containing listed flame retardant chemicals above set limits. Older inventory, used items, and products with recycled content are exempt, and the Safety Fire Commissioner could add more chemicals over time. Violators face fines up to $50,000, tripled if the violation is knowing. Realtors may care because it could affect flooring and window products used by builders, renovators, and home stagers, though resale of previously owned items is not restricted.

bills.headline: Creates a 15% state income tax credit for opening healthy food stores in less developed areas.
bills.recap: Starting in 2026, taxpayers could claim a state income tax credit worth 15% of the cost to build, renovate, buy, or lease property used to open a store selling fresh fruits and vegetables in a less developed area. Eligible stores include grocery stores, corner stores, convenience stores, farmers' markets, and small food retailers. The credit is claimed in the year the store opens, and unused amounts can carry forward five years. Realtors working in commercial sales and leasing may see more demand for retail space in designated less developed areas.
